claim: Australia introduced COVID-19 infection prevention and control measures in early 2020.
source: Australia introduced COVID-19 infection prevention and control measures in early 2020.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the timing of Australia's COVID-19 response measures, which is established knowledge about the pandemic timeline.

claim: The Australian Government Department of Health commissioned a modelled evaluation of the impact of disruptions to population breast, bowel, and cervical cancer screening programmes on cancer outcomes and cancer services.
source: To help prepare health services, the Australian Government Department of Health commissioned a modelled evaluation of the impact of disruptions to population breast, bowel, and cervical cancer screening programmes on cancer outcomes and cancer services.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the commissioning of the study, which is a factual claim about the study's origin.

claim: The Policy1 modelling platforms were used to predict outcomes for potential disruptions to cancer screening participation.
source: We used the Policy1 modelling platforms to predict outcomes for potential disruptions to cancer screening participation, covering periods of 3, 6, 9, and 12 mo.
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the tools used in the study.

claim: A 12-month screening disruption would reduce breast cancer diagnoses by 9.3% at the population level over 2020-2021.
source: We found that a 12-mo screening disruption would reduce breast cancer diagnoses (9.3% population-level reduction over 2020–2021)
evidence: This is a specific quantitative finding from the modelling study.

claim: A 12-month screening disruption would reduce colorectal cancer diagnoses by up to 12.1% over 2020-2021.
source: We found that a 12-mo screening disruption would reduce breast cancer diagnoses (9.3% population-level reduction over 2020–2021) and colorectal cancer (up to 12.1% reduction over 2020–21)
evidence: This is a specific quantitative finding from the modelling study.

claim: A 12-month screening disruption would increase cervical cancer diagnoses by up to 3.6% over 2020-2022.
source: We found that a 12-mo screening disruption would reduce breast cancer diagnoses (9.3% population-level reduction over 2020–2021) and colorectal cancer (up to 12.1% reduction over 2020–21), and increase cervical cancer diagnoses (up to 3.6% over 2020–2022)
evidence: This is a specific quantitative finding from the modelling study.

claim: Upstaging is expected for breast, cervical, and colorectal cancers with disruptions, at rates of 2%, 6.8%, and 1.4% respectively.
source: with upstaging expected for these cancer types (2, 1.4, and 6.8% for breast, cervical, and colorectal cancers, respectively).
evidence: This is a specific quantitative finding from the modelling study about cancer staging.

claim: Population cancer screening programmes aim to reduce cancer-specific mortality, complications, and side effects associated with the treatment of advanced-stage neoplasms.
source: Population cancer screening programmes aim to reduce cancer-specific mortality, complications, and side effects associated with the treatment of advanced-stage neoplasms and, in the case of bowel and cervical screening, reduce the incidence, illness, and mortality of cancers through the detection and treatment of precancerous abnormalities (Lauby-Secretan et al., 2015; Bouvard et al., 2021; Lauby-Secretan et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Bowel and cervical screening reduce the incidence, illness, and mortality of cancers through the detection and treatment of precancerous abnormalities.
source: Population cancer screening programmes aim to reduce cancer-specific mortality, complications, and side effects associated with the treatment of advanced-stage neoplasms and, in the case of bowel and cervical screening, reduce the incidence, illness, and mortality of cancers through the detection and treatment of precancerous abnormalities (Lauby-Secretan et al., 2015; Bouvard et al., 2021; Lauby-Secretan et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Breast, bowel and cervical screening programmes reduce cancer-specific deaths, with mortality benefits outweighing the risks associated with screening.
source: Breast, bowel and cervical screening programmes reduce cancer-specific deaths, with mortality benefits outweighing the risks associated with screening (Lauby-Secretan et al., 2015; Bouvard et al., 2021; Lauby-Secretan et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Australia established a national screening programme for breast cancer in 1991.
source: Australia established national screening programmes for breast and cervical cancer in 1991 and colorectal cancer in 2006 (Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, 2020a; Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, 2021c; Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, 2021a).
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by citation to an authoritative source.

claim: Australia established a national screening programme for cervical cancer in 1991.
source: Australia established national screening programmes for breast and cervical cancer in 1991 and colorectal cancer in 2006 (Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, 2020a; Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, 2021c; Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, 2021a).
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by citation to an authoritative source.

claim: Australia established a national screening programme for colorectal cancer in 2006.
source: Australia established national screening programmes for breast and cervical cancer in 1991 and colorectal cancer in 2006 (Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, 2020a; Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, 2021c; Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, 2021a).
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by citation to an authoritative source.

claim: The World Health Organization declared the COVID-19 pandemic in March 2020.
source: Following the World Health Organization's declaration of the COVID-19 pandemic, in March 2020, Australia introduced strict national and state-level infection control measures
evidence: This is established knowledge about the WHO's pandemic declaration timing.

claim: Australia introduced strict national and state-level infection control measures in March 2020, including physical and social restrictions affecting health services, business, transport, and public gatherings.
source: Following the World Health Organization's declaration of the COVID-19 pandemic, in March 2020, Australia introduced strict national and state-level infection control measures, including physical and social restrictions affecting health services, as well as business, transport, and public gatherings.
evidence: This is a factual statement about Australia's pandemic response measures.

claim: Australia's COVID-19 restrictions proved highly effective for short-term national pandemic control.
source: These restrictions proved highly effective for short-term national pandemic control, although significant outbreaks followed through returning travellers and hotel quarantine programmes (Victorian Government, 2021), subsequent new COVID variants (Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, 2021b), and ongoing variation in control measures (Sombetzki et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to government and health reports.

claim: Significant COVID-19 outbreaks followed in Australia through returning travellers and hotel quarantine programmes.
source: These restrictions proved highly effective for short-term national pandemic control, although significant outbreaks followed through returning travellers and hotel quarantine programmes (Victorian Government, 2021), subsequent new COVID variants (Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, 2021b), and ongoing variation in control measures (Sombetzki et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a government report.

claim: Modelled evaluations of COVID-impact scenarios have been undertaken by different countries to support their cancer screening programmes as they respond to the pandemic.
source: Modelled evaluations of COVID-impact scenarios have been undertaken by different countries to support their cancer screening programmes as they respond to the pandemic (Maringe et al., 2020; Burger et al., 2021; de Jonge et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The COVID-19 and Cancer Global Modelling Consortium was established to collectively conduct evaluations to support cancer control during and after the COVID-19 pandemic.
source: In parallel, collaborations within the global modelling community have been established, such as the COVID-19 and Cancer Global Modelling Consortium, to collectively conduct evaluations to support cancer control during and after the COVID-19 pandemic (COVID-19 and Cancer Global Modelling Consortium, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the consortium.

claim: In early 2020, the Australian Government Department of Health commissioned a rapid-response modelled evaluation of the health impacts of potential widespread disruptions to population breast, bowel, and cervical screening.
source: In early 2020, we were commissioned by the Australian Government Department of Health to undertake a rapid-response modelled evaluation of the health impacts of potential widespread disruptions to population breast, bowel, and cervical screening.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the commissioning of the study.

claim: This was the first time an analysis across all screening programmes had been performed in Australia.
source: This was the first time such an analysis across all screening programmes had been performed.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study approach.

claim: Simulation modelling was used to estimate outcomes for various potential disruptions to cancer screening services.
source: We used simulation modelling to estimate outcomes for various potential disruptions to cancer screening services.
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the study approach.

claim: The Policy1 modelling platform is comprehensive and validated.
source: This evaluation included detailed reporting of outcomes for different subgroups where this was requested by key stakeholders (e.g. breast screening outcomes according to whether clients were directly or indirectly impacted by screening disruptions).
evidence: This is a claim about the characteristics of the modelling platform used, supported by reference to the platform.

claim: The Policy1 platform has evaluated the clinical benefits and harms of a wide range of screening protocols, new technologies, and risk-based approaches aiming to optimise population cancer screening programmes.
source: To simulate scenarios and estimate projected outcomes, we used Policy1 which has evaluated the clinical benefits and harms of a wide range of screening protocols, new technologies, and risk-based approaches aiming to optimise population cancer screening programmes (Canfell, 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Scenarios were specified according to screening disruption duration (broadly 3, 6, 9, or 12 months) and degree (complete pauses or reduced throughput).
source: Scenarios were specified according to screening disruption duration (broadly 3, 6, 9, or 12 mo) and degree (complete pauses or reduced throughput) (Table 1).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about scenario design, with reference to a table.

claim: The BreastScreen Australia programme offers biennial (and some annual) mammographic screening to women from the age of 40 years, targeted to women aged 50-74 years.
source: The BreastScreen Australia (BSA) programme offers biennial (and some annual) mammographic screening to women from the age of 40 y, targeted to women aged 50–74 y (Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, 2020a).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the screening programme, supported by citation to an authoritative source.

claim: The BreastScreen Australia programme is administered by the eight state and territory governments under a national agreement.
source: The programme is administered by the eight state and territory governments under a national agreement.
evidence: This is a factual statement about programme administration.

claim: All abnormal screens in the BreastScreen Australia programme are assessed within the programme.
source: All abnormal screens are assessed within the programme.
evidence: This is a factual statement about programme procedures.

claim: Prior to COVID-19, participation in BreastScreen Australia by women aged 50-74 was approximately 55%.
source: Prior to COVID-19, participation by women aged 50–74 was approximately 55%, with 51% of national breast cancers detected through BreastScreen, while the proportion of clients who attended screening on schedule ranged from 60% to 84%, depending on the screening round (Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, 2020a).
evidence: This is a factual statement about pre-COVID participation rates, supported by citation.

claim: Prior to COVID-19, 51% of national breast cancers were detected through BreastScreen.
source: Prior to COVID-19, participation by women aged 50–74 was approximately 55%, with 51% of national breast cancers detected through BreastScreen, while the proportion of clients who attended screening on schedule ranged from 60% to 84%, depending on the screening round (Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, 2020a).
evidence: This is a factual statement about cancer detection rates, supported by citation.

claim: Prior to COVID-19, the proportion of BreastScreen clients who attended screening on schedule ranged from 60% to 84%, depending on the screening round.
source: Prior to COVID-19, participation by women aged 50–74 was approximately 55%, with 51% of national breast cancers detected through BreastScreen, while the proportion of clients who attended screening on schedule ranged from 60% to 84%, depending on the screening round (Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, 2020a).
evidence: This is a factual statement about screening adherence, supported by citation.

claim: The Policy1-Breast model was used to evaluate a 3-, 6-, or 12-month national-level pause commencing 1 April 2020.
source: Using the Policy1-Breast model, we evaluated a 3-, 6-, or 12-mo national-level pause (applied as an averaging of annual rates), commencing 1 April 2020.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the modelling approach.

claim: A gradual restoration of breast screening service was assumed following pause periods, returning by the seventh month to pre-COVID throughput for shorter-term pauses (3- and 6-month) and 150% of pre-COVID throughput for a longer pause (12-month).
source: We assumed a gradual restoration of service following pause periods, returning by the seventh month to pre-COVID throughput (screening capacity) for shorter-term pauses (3- and 6 mo) and 150% of pre-COVID throughput for a longer pause (12 mo), on the basis that only a year-long pause would involve expanded recovery strategies.
evidence: This is a methodological assumption used in the modelling.

claim: Opportunistic or risk-based breast screening outside the programme was assumed to be reduced by 50% during programme pause, reaching 100% on BreastScreen service resumption.
source: Opportunistic or risk-based screening outside the programme was assumed to be reduced by 50% during programme pause (due to COVID-19 social distancing requirements), reaching 100% on BreastScreen service resumption.
evidence: This is a methodological assumption used in the modelling.

claim: Policy1-Breast was revised to include a prioritisation module so that it could be applied to capacity-driven recovery scenarios.
source: For this evaluation, Policy1-Breast was revised to include a prioritisation module (see details in Supplementary file 1A) so that it could be applied to capacity-driven recovery scenarios.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about model modifications.

claim: Following breast screening service resumption, the restart strategy involved the allocation of available screens according to whether clients were newly invited or existing, their age, the period in which their appointment fell, and the time elapsed since their originally scheduled appointment.
source: Following service resumption, the restart strategy involved the allocation of available screens according to (i) whether clients were newly invited or existing, (ii) their age, (iii) the period in which their appointment fell (i.e. during the pause or during the recovery period), and (iv) the time elapsed since their originally scheduled appointment.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the prioritisation strategy modelled.

claim: Breast screening appointments were prioritised for women in the target age range of 50-74 years and to clients most overdue for screening.
source: Appointments were prioritised for women in the target age range of 50–74 y and to clients most overdue for screening.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the prioritisation strategy modelled.

claim: The National Bowel Cancer Screening Program provides biennial primary screening using an immunochemical faecal occult blood test to all Australians aged 50-74 years via the national postal service.
source: The National Bowel Cancer Screening Program (NBCSP) provides biennial primary screening, using an immunochemical faecal occult blood test (iFOBT), to all Australians aged 50–74 y via the national postal service.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the screening programme.

claim: The bowel screening kit is self-administered at home and, if positive, a follow-up colonoscopy is recommended for diagnostic investigation.
source: The screening kit is self-administered at home and, if positive, a follow-up colonoscopy is recommended for diagnostic investigation.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the screening procedure.

claim: Prior to COVID-19, participation in the National Bowel Cancer Screening Program was approximately 44%.
source: Prior to COVID-19, participation was approximately 44%, with 62% of individuals with a positive iFOBT reported as completing a colonoscopy (Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, 2021c).
evidence: This is a factual statement about pre-COVID participation rates, supported by citation.

claim: Prior to COVID-19, 62% of individuals with a positive iFOBT completed a colonoscopy.
source: Prior to COVID-19, participation was approximately 44%, with 62% of individuals with a positive iFOBT reported as completing a colonoscopy (Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, 2021c).
evidence: This is a factual statement about follow-up rates, supported by citation.

claim: The Policy1-Bowel model was used to evaluate a 3-, 6-, or 12-month national-level pause commencing 1 April 2020.
source: Using the Policy1-Bowel model, we evaluated a 3-, 6-, or 12-mo national-level pause, commencing 1 April 2020 during which time we assumed that no screening invitations or kits were sent or processed and all primary screening and diagnostic or surveillance colonoscopies associated with the NBCSP were halted.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the modelling approach.

claim: During bowel screening pause periods, it was assumed that no screening invitations or kits were sent or processed and all primary screening and diagnostic or surveillance colonoscopies associated with the NBCSP were halted.
source: Using the Policy1-Bowel model, we evaluated a 3-, 6-, or 12-mo national-level pause, commencing 1 April 2020 during which time we assumed that no screening invitations or kits were sent or processed and all primary screening and diagnostic or surveillance colonoscopies associated with the NBCSP were halted.
evidence: This is a methodological assumption used in the modelling.

claim: It was assumed that individuals missing a bowel screen during the pause would be screened at the next screening round, 2 years later.
source: It was assumed that individuals missing a screen during the pause would be screened at the next screening round, 2 y later.
evidence: This is a methodological assumption used in the modelling.

claim: Bowel screening outcomes have been estimated for people aged 50-74 years eligible for screening in 2020 and 2021, comprising 7.1 million people (3.5 million men and 3.6 million women).
source: Outcomes have been estimated for the affected cohorts only, that is, among people aged 50–74 y eligible for screening in 2020 and 2021. This cohort comprises 7.1 million people; 3.5 million men and 3.6 million women.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the study population.

claim: The National Cervical Screening Program is provided to women aged 25-74 years and usually involves a visit to primary care.
source: The National Cervical Screening Program (NSCP) is provided to women aged 25–74 y and usually involves a visit to primary care.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the screening programme.

claim: Modelled cervical screening participation was updated to reflect National Cancer Screening Register data indicating that 53.6% of women had already attended for their first HPV test.
source: As part of this evaluation, we updated modelled screening participation to reflect National Cancer Screening Register data (Supplementary file 1B), indicating that 53.6% of women had already attended for their first HPV test, and therefore were not due to attend for routine screening again until at least December 2022.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about data used in the model.

claim: 6-, 9-, or 12-month disruptions to cervical screening participation in 2020 were evaluated, with participation during these periods being 50%, 75%, and 90% lower, respectively, than would otherwise have been expected.
source: We evaluated 6-, 9-, or 12-mo disruptions to screening participation in 2020, with participation during these periods being 50, 75, and 90% lower, respectively, than would otherwise have been expected.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the scenarios modelled.

claim: For the 2-year period 2020-2021, screening pauses of any duration would lead to an overall reduction in population-level invasive breast cancer diagnosis for women aged 50-74 years.
source: For the 2-y period 2020–2021, we estimate that screening pauses of any duration would lead to an overall reduction in population-level invasive breast cancer diagnosis for women aged 50–74 y, noting that the estimated reduction in cancer incidence was comparable (~9%) between a 6-mo pause with pre-COVID throughout during recovery and a 12-mo pause with 150% throughput during recovery (Table 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the modelling study, with reference to a table.

claim: The estimated reduction in breast cancer incidence was comparable (~9%) between a 6-month pause with pre-COVID throughput during recovery and a 12-month pause with 150% throughput during recovery.
source: For the 2-y period 2020–2021, we estimate that screening pauses of any duration would lead to an overall reduction in population-level invasive breast cancer diagnosis for women aged 50–74 y, noting that the estimated reduction in cancer incidence was comparable (~9%) between a 6-mo pause with pre-COVID throughout during recovery and a 12-mo pause with 150% throughput during recovery (Table 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the modelling study, with reference to a table.

claim: All breast screening scenarios would lead to reduced population-level rates of screen-detected cancers and interval cancers, reduced programme sensitivity, and more advanced tumour stage at diagnosis.
source: All scenarios would lead to reduced population-level rates of screen-detected cancers and interval cancers, reduced programme sensitivity, and more advanced tumour stage at diagnosis.
evidence: This is a finding from the modelling study.

claim: With a 12-month breast screening pause, there is an estimated 10% difference in population-level invasive breast cancer diagnoses among women aged 50-74 between 2020-2021 (270 per 100,000 women) and 2022-2023 (296 per 100,000 women).
source: Longer-term fluctuations in clinical and programme outcomes are also expected; for example, with a 12-mo pause we estimate a 10% difference in population-level invasive breast cancer diagnoses among women aged 50–74 between 2020 and 2021 (270 per 100,000 women) and 2022–2023 (296 per 100,000 women) (Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from the modelling study.

claim: Estimated breast screening intervals ranged from a median of 107 weeks for a 3-month pause through to 130 weeks for a 12-month pause.
source: Estimated screening intervals ranged from a median of 107 wk for a 3-mo pause through to 130 wk for a 12-mo pause, with a median of 154 wk for women who missed screens during the pause (Supplementary file 1E).
evidence: This is a finding from the modelling study.

claim: Breast screening recall rates are predicted to fluctuate over time under various pause scenarios, ranging from 5.3% (3-month pause) to 5.6% (12-month pause).
source: Recall rates are predicted to fluctuate over time under various pause scenarios, ranging from 5.3% (3-mo pause) to 5.6% (12-mo pause) (Table 3), most likely due to an increasing proportion of first-round screening during recovery.
evidence: This is a finding from the modelling study, with reference to a table.

claim: All three bowel screening scenarios illustrated a decrease in cancer diagnoses and cancers being diagnosed at a later stage in the screening cohort compared to the status quo.
source: All three scenarios illustrated a decrease in cancer diagnoses and cancers being diagnosed at a later stage in the screening cohort compared to the status quo.
evidence: This is a finding from the modelling study.

claim: Across the modelled bowel screening scenarios, colorectal cancer diagnoses decreased in 2020-2021 by 583-2549 cases (2.8-12.1% decrease).
source: Across the modelled scenarios, colorectal cancer diagnoses decreased in 2020–2021 by 583–2549 cases (2.8–12.1% decrease).
evidence: This is a finding from the modelling study.

claim: The modelled bowel screening disruptions resulted in a stage shift, with up to 891 cases which would have been diagnosed but instead progressed to a later stage with lower survival.
source: The modelled disruptions resulted in a stage shift, with up to 891 cases which would have been diagnosed but instead progressed to a later stage with lower survival.
evidence: This is a finding from the modelling study.

claim: The NBCSP-related colonoscopies that would not be conducted in 2020 due to the 3-, 6-, and 12-month disruptions would be 19,151, 38,335, and 76,125 respectively.
source: The NBCSP-related colonoscopies that would not be conducted in 2020 due to the 3-, 6-, and 12-mo disruptions would be 19,151, 38,335, and 76,125 respectively.
evidence: This is a finding from the modelling study.

claim: A 12-month pause to bowel screening would lead to an additional 7140 colorectal cancer cases over 2020-2050.
source: This analysis found that a 12-mo pause to screening would lead to an additional 7140 colorectal cancer cases over 2020–2050.
evidence: This is a finding from the modelling study.

claim: All three cervical screening scenarios resulted in an increase in cancer diagnoses and cancers being diagnosed at a later stage among screening-age women compared to what would have been expected in the absence of any disruption.
source: All three scenarios resulted in an increase in cancer diagnoses and cancers being diagnosed at a later stage among screening-age women compared to what would have been expected in the absence of any disruption.
evidence: This is a finding from the modelling study.

claim: The increase in cervical cancer cases over 2020-2022 ranged from 21 to 69 cases (1.1-3.6% increase).
source: The increase in cancer cases over 2020–2022 ranged from 21 to 69 cases (1.1–3.6% increase).
evidence: This is a finding from the modelling study.

claim: Most (57-63%) of the additional cervical cancers were diagnosed among women 30-49 years old.
source: Most (57–63%) of the additional cancers were diagnosed among women 30–49 y.
evidence: This is a finding from the modelling study.

claim: Women aged 30-39 years and 40-49 years were the age groups where the percentage increase in cervical cancers was largest (1.1-4.1% and 1.2-4.3% respectively).
source: Women aged 30–39 y and 40–49 y were also the age groups where the percentage increase in cancers was largest (although still relatively small: 1.1–4.1% and 1.2–4.3% in women aged 30–39 and 40–49 y, respectively).
evidence: This is a finding from the modelling study.

claim: The model predicted that disruptions to routine primary cervical screening would lead to 6-18 cervical cancers being diagnosed at regional stage in 2021-2022, rather than as localised cancers in 2020.
source: The model predicted that disruptions to routine primary screening would lead to 6–18 cervical cancers being diagnosed at regional stage in 2021–2022, rather than as localised cancers in 2020; and 3–9 cervical cancers being diagnosed at distant stage in 2021–2022, rather than at regional stage in 2020.
evidence: This is a finding from the modelling study.

claim: The model predicted that disruptions to routine primary cervical screening would lead to 3-9 cervical cancers being diagnosed at distant stage in 2021-2022, rather than at regional stage in 2020.
source: The model predicted that disruptions to routine primary screening would lead to 6–18 cervical cancers being diagnosed at regional stage in 2021–2022, rather than as localised cancers in 2020; and 3–9 cervical cancers being diagnosed at distant stage in 2021–2022, rather than at regional stage in 2020.
evidence: This is a finding from the modelling study.

claim: An estimated 30-97 women would be affected by delays in cervical cancer diagnosis due to disruptions to routine screening in 2020.
source: Considering both additional cervical cancers and those which were diagnosed at a later stage due to disruptions to cervical screening, an estimated 30–97 women would be affected by delays in diagnosis due to disruptions to routine screening in 2020.
evidence: This is a finding from the modelling study.

claim: Disruptions to primary cervical screening in 2020 are estimated to result in 17,680-47,868 fewer women attending for a colposcopy in 2020 (17.4-47.2% reduction).
source: Disruptions to primary screening in 2020 are estimated to result in 17,680–47,868 fewer women attending for a colposcopy in 2020 (17.4–47.2% reduction) as a result of their primary screening or triage test.
evidence: This is a finding from the modelling study.

claim: For similar disruption scenarios, markedly different impacts are estimated for each screening programme.
source: We present outcomes estimated in 2020 for a range of potential disruptions to national population cancer screening programmes for breast, cervical, and colorectal cancer, including population-level changes in cancer diagnoses and staging. For similar disruption scenarios, we estimate markedly different impacts for each programme.
evidence: This is a summary finding from the modelling study.

claim: For a 6-month screening disruption, reduced diagnoses of breast cancer (9.4% population-level reduction over 2020-2021, with 100% throughput) and colorectal cancer (up to 5.8% reduction over 2020-21) and increased cervical cancer diagnoses (up to 1.1% over 2020-2022) were estimated, with less marked upstaging compared to a 12-month disruption.
source: For a 6-mo screening disruption we estimated reduced diagnoses of breast cancer (9.4% population-level reduction over 2020–2021, with 100% throughput) and colorectal cancer (up to 5.8% reduction over 2020–21) and increased cervical cancer diagnoses (up to 1.1% over 2020–2022), with less marked upstaging compared to a 12-mo disruption.
evidence: This is a summary finding from the modelling study.

claim: Findings were most marked for bowel screening, for which short-term upstaging and reduced cancer incidence was expected to lead to a significant number of additional colorectal cancer cases over the lifetime of the affected cohort.
source: Findings were most marked for bowel screening, for which short-term upstaging and reduced cancer incidence was expected to lead to a significant number of additional colorectal cancer cases over the lifetime of the affected cohort.
evidence: This is a summary finding from the modelling study.

claim: For cervical screening, relative and absolute increases in cancer are expected to be less than for breast and colorectal cancer.
source: For cervical screening, relative and absolute increases in cancer are expected to be less than for breast and colorectal cancer.
evidence: This is a summary finding from the modelling study.

claim: The lower impact on cervical cancer is likely due to COVID-19 impacts coinciding with lower participation under status quo because the programme recently transitioned to a longer screening interval, along with the lower burden of disease due to prevention through both screening and widespread uptake of HPV vaccination (80% three-dose coverage among females aged 14-15).
source: This is likely due to COVID-19 impacts coinciding with lower participation under status quo because the programme recently transitioned to a longer screening interval, along with the lower burden of disease due to prevention through both screening and widespread uptake of HPV vaccination (80% three-dose coverage among females aged 14–15) (Australian Government, Department of Health, 2022a).
evidence: This is an interpretation of findings, with citation supporting the HPV vaccination coverage statistic.

claim: The modelling platforms used are established for breast, colorectal, and HPV/cervical cancer natural history and screening in Australia, and are well calibrated and validated to the Australian context using high-quality published data.
source: We used established modelling platforms for breast, colorectal, and HPV/cervical cancer natural history and screening in Australia, which were already well calibrated and validated to the Australian context using high-quality published data, including detailed governmental screening reports.
evidence: This is a statement about the study methods and their quality.

claim: Prior investment into these modelling platforms facilitated the rapid response modelling required in the face of a crisis.
source: Prior investment into these modelling platforms facilitated the rapid response modelling required in the face of a crisis; the evaluations reported highlight the importance of ongoing investment into comprehensive, well-calibrated and validated population predictive models that can be quickly harnessed for critical decision-making as needed for disruptions such as the COVID-19 pandemic and other potential disruptions due to major social, public health, or natural disasters as are increasingly common due to climate change (Bureau of Meteorology, 2020).
evidence: This is a statement about the value of the modelling infrastructure, with citation supporting the climate change reference.

claim: Scenarios were defined in simple terms, modeling single, continuous periods of national disruption, though in practice screening participation would likely fluctuate by time and place.
source: Scenarios were by necessity defined in simple terms. For example, we modelled single, continuous periods of national disruption but, in practice, screening participation would likely fluctuate by time and place in line with local outbreaks and pandemic control measures.
evidence: This is a statement about study limitations.

claim: The modelled estimates do not account for changes in diagnostic and treatment services due to COVID-19 which have since been observed.
source: Modelled estimates will likely include some biases. We do not account for changes in diagnostic and treatment services due to COVID-19 which have since been observed (Australian Government, Cancer Australia, 2021).
evidence: This is a statement about study limitations, with citation to observed data.

claim: Medicare Benefits Schedule claims data from 2020 indicates a 4% reduction in breast diagnostic services and 6% reduction in breast cancer-related surgical procedures.
source: For example, Medicare Benefits Schedule claims data from 2020 indicates a 4% reduction in breast diagnostic services and 6% reduction in breast cancer-related surgical procedures, and for colorectal cancer a 13% reduction in diagnostic services (mostly colonoscopies) and 1% reduced surgical procedures.
evidence: This is a factual statement about observed data.

claim: Medicare Benefits Schedule claims data from 2020 indicates a 13% reduction in colorectal cancer diagnostic services (mostly colonoscopies) and 1% reduced surgical procedures.
source: For example, Medicare Benefits Schedule claims data from 2020 indicates a 4% reduction in breast diagnostic services and 6% reduction in breast cancer-related surgical procedures, and for colorectal cancer a 13% reduction in diagnostic services (mostly colonoscopies) and 1% reduced surgical procedures.
evidence: This is a factual statement about observed data.

claim: The Australian cervical and bowel screening programmes continued to operate continuously through 2020.
source: The Australian cervical and bowel screening programmes continued to operate continuously through 2020 (and since), while BreastScreen services paused nationally from March to late April/early May 2020, resuming thereafter.
evidence: This is a factual statement about observed programme operations.

claim: BreastScreen services paused nationally from March to late April/early May 2020, resuming thereafter.
source: The Australian cervical and bowel screening programmes continued to operate continuously through 2020 (and since), while BreastScreen services paused nationally from March to late April/early May 2020, resuming thereafter.
evidence: This is a factual statement about observed programme operations.

claim: There was an overall 34% reduction in screening tests across the three programmes comprising over 1 million (1,035,710) fewer breast, bowel, and cervix tests in age-targeted Australian populations in January to September 2020 compared to January to September 2019.
